There's no need to rush out and buy everything at once. I built up my tools over many years, just picking them up as needed. Everyone has their own likes/dislikes, but the following are some points based on my experience:

  • Take a trip to your local pawn shop once in a while. You can get some awesome deals.
  • Utility knives and measuring tapes -- buy in bulk. Keep them all over the house because going to the basement sucks when you just need it for second.
  • Pencils!!!! God knows how many times I've had to stop a job and waste 10 mins looking for a pencil to mark a cut. I think my house eats them. Have two in every drawer and toolbox.
  • Corded tools have more torque, are more reliable and don't run out of juice. Extension cords are cheap. Batteries are expensive. A cordless drill and driver are handy, but only for light jobs.
  • Everyone always told me to buy high quality. It'll pay for itself over time. I always consider how much use it's going to get. I have the world's cheapest POS jigsaw. I only make about half a dozen cuts every other year. If it breaks, it's disposable. Not saying don't buy quality, just invest according to your need. Hammers, drivers, wrenches, pliers; well worth spending money on things you use a lot and will last for decades. Pipecutter? Well how often are you gonna replumb the sink?
  • It's nice to have a modular screwdriver for light work around the house, but get yourself a quality set of fixed shaft ones for real work.
  • Buy a good mitre saw with a stand and a construction site (folding) table saw. I end up using these A LOT. Unless you've got a lot of shop space being able to fold them up and stow them is great. They don't need to be high end unless you're thinking of going pro, but good enough that you can depend on them to be accurate and long lived.
  • I've tried many different pegboards and organization systems, but what I've found works best is to modularize. I have my plumbing box, painting kit, electrical, basic handtools all in seperate toolboxes. It leads to some duplication, but it beats having to graze through your tools when you have task oriented tools grouped together.
  • Get a Richard's 7in1 painting tool. Seriously, I could build a house with that little fucker.
  • A quality paint set up. Brushes, roller, tray, etc. It's worth spending the money to get good stuff as you'll use it a hundred times and there's nothing more indicating than a cheap vacuformed paint tray. Clean it well after every use and it'll last for ages.
  • Get your wife a toolbox and some basic tools. This one obviously depends on your wife/family. It not only makes her feel like she can do stuff, it also keeps her from fucking around your toolbox so you can't find the tool you need when you need it. My missus even has a cute little 8oz hammer; so cute you wanna snuggle it (though I can drive a nail faster with the 7in1 painting tool).
  • Get a good set of hex wrenches. Every flat pack you assemble for the next 20 yrs will go better. I still haven't found an ideal set, but the best so far is set of modular driver bits, long ones if you can find them. Nice to be able to throw them into a cordless driver.
  • Someone said how-to books. I'd say it's a waste of money. The internet is way more specific to the exact problem you are trying to solve. Sure, maybe if you're a prepper and want to be ready when SHTF, but not required for home maintenance IMNSHO.
  • As you already have a compressor, air tools are awesome. Brad nailers, staple guns, paint sprayers, inflation gauges, torque wrenches... giddy up. Love my air tools.
  • Your ladder needs will vary depending on the house, but you'll never regret having a good 6' step ladder.
  • Good extension cords. Silicone if you can find them.
  • Buy the new expanding hoses, but make sure they have brass fittings. They are way more flexible and store better than the old ones. Just don't buy the ones with plastic end fittings. Learned that one the hard way - they only last about a season and can't be fixed.

Disagree about cordless power tools, the advances made are not applied to corded tools and there is no equivalent to a impact driver, at least at the consumer level.
